flashcards.title: Yamas
flashcards.short_answer: Ethical restraints on "how we relate to others".
flashcards.definition: Yamas are the social disciplines or restraints that guide our interactions with the world around us with specific practices: (Ahimsa, Satya, Asteya, Brahmacarya, and Aparigraha) that help us act with awareness rather than reacting out of habit or vice. Sometimes called the "Do nots".

flashcards.title: Niyamas
flashcards.short_answer: Personal observances or "how we relate to ourselves".
flashcards.definition: These are internal practices meant to improve our own character and being. They consist of Sauca, Santosha, Tapas, Svadhyaya, and Isvara-pranidhana. These habits, behaviors, and observances outline guidance for healthy living, spiritual enlightenment, and existence with liberation and ease. These are the "To Do's".

flashcards.title: Asana
flashcards.short_answer: Physical postures; literally meaning "to sit" or "being seated".
flashcards.definition: Originally referring to sitting with a master to receive knowledge, it has evolved into the physical practice of postures. The goal is to find a balance between Sthira (steadiness/effort) and Sukha (comfort/ease) so the body is alert but unstressed.

flashcards.title: Pranayama
flashcards.short_answer: Breath control and the regulation of life force.
flashcards.definition: This practice involves joining the breath with movement to integrate the body and mind. It includes techniques like Ujjayi (calming) or Kapalabhati (energizing) to help the mind become slower, deeper, and more focused.

flashcards.title: Pratyahara
flashcards.short_answer: Withdrawal of the senses; not chasing the "shiny object".
flashcards.definition: It is the practice of filtering out external distractions to focus inward. For example, when a siren goes off during savasana, you use Pratyahara to stay present in your practice rather than following the noise.

flashcards.title: Dharana
flashcards.short_answer: Concentration; holding the mind in one direction.
flashcards.definition: We create the conditions to focus the mind's attention on a single object, like the breath, a candle, or a mandala. This prevents the "monkey mind" from jumping in many different directions.

flashcards.title: Dhyana
flashcards.short_answer: Meditation; a continuous flow of concentration.
flashcards.definition: In this state, the mind moves in one direction like a quiet river. You perceive an object and focus only on it, forming a deep communication where nothing else is happening.

flashcards.title: Samadhi
flashcards.short_answer: Union; becoming one with the object of meditation.
flashcards.definition: This is the experience of realizing non-dualistic existence, seeing things clearly without the Maya (illusion). It is pure flow where you are no longer a separate physical creature but are united with the divine or the fabric of the universe.

flashcards.title: Ahimsa
flashcards.short_answer: Non-violence; do no harm.
flashcards.definition: This is the practice of justice and non-violence toward all beings. In yoga class, it means finding a balance with Satya—for example, not pushing yourself or a student so hard that it causes injury, but also not avoiding the truth of where growth is needed.

flashcards.title: Satya
flashcards.short_answer: Truthfulness.
flashcards.definition: This involves being honest with ourselves and others. As a teacher, it means providing "radical candor" or a "+1 nudge" to help students see their flaws and grow, provided the feedback comes from a sincere, caring place.

flashcards.title: Asteya
flashcards.short_answer: Non-stealing.
flashcards.definition: Beyond just not taking physical objects, it involves not stealing others' time or energy. It is a reminder to avoid vices and distractions, focusing instead on what we have earned.

flashcards.title: Brahmacarya
flashcards.short_answer: Responsible behavior; moderation of the senses.
flashcards.definition: Often interpreted as respect for family life and not overdoing sexual pleasure, it is a subtle call to move toward the truth through responsible, disciplined behavior.

flashcards.title: Aparigraha
flashcards.short_answer: Non-greed or non-attachment; only taking what is necessary.
flashcards.definition: This means not taking advantage of a situation and only taking what you have earned. It is the practice of non-coveting, which helps us stay away from addiction and ego-centrism.

flashcards.title: Sauca
flashcards.short_answer: Purity, cleanliness, and clarity of body and mind.
flashcards.definition: Purity of mind, speech and body. Keeping physical cleanliness through asanas, pranayama, and proper eating, and maintaining cleanliness in our physical environment. Purity of speech comes from being truthful and using words that are not hurtful, or distressing to others or self. Purity of thoughts through reflection, meditation, and calmness. It is about getting rid of "rubbish" in the mind and body through healthy habits.

flashcards.title: Santosha
flashcards.short_answer: Contentment; being okay with what is.
flashcards.definition: To be content with what we already have and to accept outcomes even when they don't meet our expectations. It is the appreciation of our current situation rather than focusing on how we wish it to be.

flashcards.title: Tapas
flashcards.short_answer: The passion, motivation and discipline that drives spiritual or physical practice.
flashcards.definition: The activity of "heating" the body through asana and pranayama to cleanse it. Includes the discipline and actions toward spiritual rituals and healthy habits, to sustain a healthy lifestyle and burn away impurities physically and spiritually.

flashcards.title: Svadhyaya
flashcards.short_answer: The practice of self-study, self-examination, and spiritual inquiry.
flashcards.definition: The study of ancient texts and the examination of one's own inner dialogue. It is an inquiry into who is "living in you" and identifying the labels we carry that are not our true identity. It is the endless pursuit of learning about ourselves and spiritual frameworks.

flashcards.title: Isvara-pranidhana
flashcards.short_answer: Devotion to the "absolute Brahma", who is free from all hindrances and karma. Devotion to a higher power.
flashcards.definition: Some interpretations mean to "lay all your actions at the feet of God" by offering the "fruits of your devotion" to something larger than yourself. It is the realization and acceptance of the part of ourselves that does not change, and surrendering to the divine part of us that is unaffected by our samskara.

flashcards.title: Yoga
flashcards.short_answer: To "yoke" or "union" - to become one with our core essence.
flashcards.definition: Yoga is a vast group of physical, mental, spiritual practices and philosophy originating in ancient India, aimed at controlling body and mind in order to attain liberation (moksha), health and connection with the universe. Yoga means to unify with all possible states of awareness, whether ordinary or extraordinary.

flashcards.title: Brahman
flashcards.short_answer: The supreme, universal reality underlying all existence.
flashcards.definition: Brahman is the ultimate, supreme reality - the infinite divine ground of all matter, energy, time, and space in the universe. It is the uncaused cause of everything, pervading every part of existence while also transcending it entirely.

flashcards.title: Atman
flashcards.short_answer: The true, immortal self or soul within each of us.
flashcards.definition: Atman is the true, immortal self or soul of a living being - not the physical body, mind, ego, or emotions, but the silent, unchanging witness residing within every creature. Its true nature is pure consciousness and eternity: it does not die when the body dies, it simply changes form.

flashcards.title: Lord Krishna
flashcards.short_answer: Revered in yoga as Yogeshvara, the Lord of Yoga.
flashcards.definition: Krishna is revered in yoga as Yogeshvara (the Lord of Yoga), the supreme teacher who defines yoga not just as physical postures but as the art of living, mental steadiness, and union with the divine. In the Bhagavad Gita, he teaches the warrior Arjuna the four core paths of yoga - Karma, Bhakti, Jnana, and Dhyana - as valid routes to liberation.

flashcards.title: The Four Yogas
flashcards.short_answer: Four classical paths to spiritual growth taught by Krishna in the Bhagavad Gita.
flashcards.definition: In the Bhagavad Gita, Krishna teaches four main paths toward spiritual realization: Karma Yoga (selfless action), Bhakti Yoga (devotion), Jnana Yoga (knowledge/self-inquiry), and Dhyana Yoga (meditation). Each suits a different personality, but all lead toward the same goal of union with the divine.

flashcards.title: Karma Yoga
flashcards.short_answer: The path of selfless action.
flashcards.definition: Karma Yoga is performing one's duties without attachment to the results or personal gain. Krishna defines yoga itself through this path as samatva (evenness of mind) and skill in action - acting with excellence and steadiness rather than for reward.

flashcards.title: Bhakti Yoga
flashcards.short_answer: The path of devotion.
flashcards.definition: Bhakti Yoga is directing complete love, surrender, and remembrance toward the divine - which Krishna calls the highest form of yoga. It's often expressed through prayer, chanting, and worship, emphasizing an open heart as the route to spiritual connection.

flashcards.title: Jnana Yoga
flashcards.short_answer: The path of knowledge and self-inquiry.
flashcards.definition: Jnana Yoga is the path of wisdom - discriminating between the temporary, material body and the eternal spiritual self (Atman) through study, reflection, and self-inquiry. It is often considered the most intellectually demanding of the four paths.

flashcards.title: Dhyana Yoga
flashcards.short_answer: The path of meditation.
flashcards.definition: Dhyana Yoga is controlling the restless mind through disciplined focus, breath, and inner meditation. It is the meditative path among the four yogas Krishna teaches in the Bhagavad Gita.

flashcards.title: Karma
flashcards.short_answer: The law of action - our deeds and intentions shape our future.
flashcards.definition: Karma is the principle that our actions and the intentions behind them shape future outcomes. Right action alone isn't enough - the thought and intention behind it matter too, since karma accounts for both.

flashcards.title: Samsara
flashcards.short_answer: The cycle of birth, death, and rebirth.
flashcards.definition: Samsara is the ongoing cycle of being reborn into another life, the quality of which is shaped by one's karma from this life. The cycle can be broken through pure devotion (bhakti) to the divine.

flashcards.title: Moksha
flashcards.short_answer: Liberation from the cycle of rebirth - the supreme goal.
flashcards.definition: Moksha is the freedom achieved by releasing attachment to the rewards of one's actions, breaking the cycle of samsara. It is considered the supreme goal of yoga and Hindu philosophy.

flashcards.title: Maya
flashcards.short_answer: The illusion of a separate, purely physical existence.
flashcards.definition: Maya is the state of living inside the illusion that life is only physical and separate - dualistic thinking. Maya is often likened to "magic," a veil that hides the deeper unity of existence.

flashcards.title: Nirvana
flashcards.short_answer: The liberated state once the cycle of rebirth is broken.
flashcards.definition: Nirvana is the state of existence reached once the cycle of samsara is broken - union with the divine. It is the Buddhist term for this state, while Samadhi is the Hindu equivalent.

flashcards.title: Prakriti
flashcards.short_answer: The base energy that forms all of nature.
flashcards.definition: Prakriti is the fundamental energy or matter that makes up all of nature, both physical and mental. It is the raw material from which the three gunas arise.

flashcards.title: Gunas
flashcards.short_answer: The three qualities of mind and nature: tamas, rajas, and sattva.
flashcards.definition: The gunas are the three forces at play in the mind that shape how we see and react to reality. At any moment we are a blend of all three - tamas, rajas, and sattva - each present to a different degree. The goal in yoga is to cultivate sattva as the dominant guna, though there are times each guna has its place.

flashcards.title: Tamas
flashcards.short_answer: The guna of inertia, dullness, and ignorance.
flashcards.definition: Tamas is the guna of inertia and unconscious ignorance - acting purely out of habit without awareness of one's actions or their effects. A tamas-dominant mind tends toward low energy, procrastination, and being easily discouraged.

flashcards.title: Rajas
flashcards.short_answer: The guna of activity, restlessness, and craving.
flashcards.definition: Rajas is the guna of unleashed energy - the "monkey mind" of racing thoughts: desire, worry, resentment, and competition. A rajas-dominant mind craves reward for its actions and can chase power, money, or status.

flashcards.title: Sattva
flashcards.short_answer: The guna of clarity, balance, and calm awareness.
flashcards.definition: Sattva is the guna of a calm, clear, aware mind - self-controlled not through effort but through the clarity that comes with unity of purpose and character. A sattva-dominant mind seeks no reward for its actions and senses the unity connecting all beings.

flashcards.title: Samskara
flashcards.short_answer: The mental filter or lens, shaped by past experience, through which we perceive reality.
flashcards.definition: Samskara refers to the subtle impressions left in the mind by our past thoughts, emotions, and actions. These accumulated impressions form a kind of lens or filter that colors how we perceive and react to the present moment - we rarely see things freshly, but through the conditioning of what came before. Yoga practice (asana, meditation, self-inquiry) is one way to become aware of these patterns and gradually loosen their grip, allowing clearer perception.
